Here's the engineered plan. Core idea: **topic becomes a first-class concept, every knowledge artifact is scoped to (user, topic), bots are bound to a topic, and every read/write tool takes an optional `scope` arg that defaults to the bot's own topic.** That single abstraction unlocks default isolation + agent-driven cross-topic agency without sprinkling special cases. ## 1. The mental model ``` Channel (phone/discord channel) └─ Bot (identity, prompt, allowed tools, persona) └─ Topic (the data partition) └─ Knowledge artifacts (memories, themes, watch items, observations, distillations) ``` - **Channel → Bot** is the routing key. User messages a specific number/channel; that determines which bot answers. - **Bot → Topic** is 1:1 *for now*, but the FK lives on the bot, not on the topic — so later you can point two bots at one topic ("coach" and "weekly summarizer" both look at career), or one bot at many ("super-agent that holds two topics") without schema change. - **Topic** is the unit of data partitioning. It owns no behavior — just an id, a name, a created_at, and a description string that appears in the bot's system prompt. This is intentionally minimal. Topic is *not* hierarchical, *not* tag-style multi-membership, *not* per-message. One artifact, one topic. Cross-topic visibility comes from query scope, not from sharing rows. ## 2. Schema changes New table: ``` topics (id, name, slug, description, created_at) ``` `topic_id` (NOT NULL after backfill) added to: - `memories`, `themes`, `watch_items`, `observations`, `distillations` - `scheduled_jobs`, `scheduled_tasks` - `bridge_candidates`, `bridge_paths` (if you keep these cross-bot, they need to be either topic-scoped or explicitly cross-topic — see §4) - `messages` (so a transcript can be filtered to the bot that owns it) - `bot_turns` - `tool_calls` (so audits are clean per-bot) - `feedback` **OOB is the one tricky table.** Some entries are global ("don't talk about my mother's death, ever, anywhere"), some are topic-bound ("don't bring up my last job in coaching context"). Add `topic_id NULL` to `out_of_bounds`: NULL = global, set = scoped. The delivery-time guardrail queries `topic_id = $bot_topic OR topic_id IS NULL`. This is the cleanest expression of the user's intent. **Users stay global.** No `topic_id` on users — a person is a person across topics. Saved to `docs/multi-agent-architecture.md`. The doc lands on these answers to your questions: **Topic vs agent scoping (you leaned topic — confirmed).** Knowledge artifacts partition by `topic_id`. Bot identity lives as an attribution column (`recorded_by_bot_id`) where it matters. The reasoning: topic outlives bot (you'll version/replace bots without wanting to migrate data), it matches how users think ("career stuff" not "coach stuff"), and it leaves the door open for two bots sharing a topic later without a migration. Bot-vs-bot heterogeneity within a topic is a *prompt* problem, not a *partition* problem. **Status concept.** New `topic_status` table keyed by `(topic, user)`. Each bot can only write its own topic's status; all statuses for the current user are injected into every bot's system prompt automatically — no tool call required for the read path. Per-user not per-pair so non-dyadic agents work later. Headline + body, kept short by contract so the prompt budget doesn't balloon. **Config split.** Behavior (prompts, tool gates, crisis handler) stays in code. Identity registration (topics, channels, bots-as-rows-pointing-at-code) lives in data. The `bots` table is a thin pointer so ops can rebind channels without a deploy, but the prompt itself is versioned with source. **Migration to "relationship" topic.** Phase 0 in §13: create topic, create bot row, create channel rows, add `topic_id`/`bot_id` columns nullable, backfill, set NOT NULL. Pure refactor — mediator behaves identically after. The doc closes with six **Decisions to confirm** (§15) — those are the spots I made a call but where I'd want a sanity check before any code lands. Worth scanning those first.

I just pulled the real schema and the answer is more nuanced than the doc reflects. There are actually **three pre-existing scoping modes**, and my doc glossed over them by treating everything as uniformly user-bound. Looking at the actual columns in `0001_init.sql`: | Table | Today's scoping | What that means | |---|---|---| | `memories` | `about_user_id` **nullable** | A memory can be about Maya, about Liam, or about both/the relationship (NULL) | | `observations` | `about_user_id` **nullable** | Same — per-person or shared/relationship-level | | `themes` | **no user FK at all** | Themes are pair-level by definition; both partners share them | | `watch_items` | `owner_user_id` **NOT NULL** | Strictly per-user — whose watch item | | `out_of_bounds` | `owner_id` **NOT NULL** | Strictly per-user — whose wish | | `scheduled_jobs` | `user_id` nullable | Per-user or unattached | So the system already distinguishes: 1. **Per-person** (the artifact is about/owned by exactly one user — Maya, Liam) 2. **Shared/relationship** (about both, represented by NULL on the nullable FK) 3. **Pair-by-default** (themes — no user concept at all, always shared) My doc treated this dimension as invisible and just added `topic_ids` on top. That's incomplete. The right model is **two orthogonal axes**: - **Topic** (which domain — career / relationship / …) — new - **About-whom** (one person / shared / pair-level) — existing, needs to be preserved For a **non-dyadic bot** (e.g. a coach with one user), the "shared" and "pair-level" modes don't exist — every artifact has `about_user_id` set to the one user. The schema already supports this: it's the dyadic mediator that *uses* the NULL mode, not the schema that mandates it. So multi-bot doesn't require schema change here, but the **hot context builder and tool semantics need to be aware** of "about-whom" per bot: - Mediator's builder bins artifacts into three buckets (about A / about B / shared) - Coach's builder has one bucket (about the user) It also has consequences for `topic_status`: - Mediator probably wants a *pair-level* status in addition to per-user — "the relationship is in X state" — which means `topic_status.user_id` may need to be nullable (NULL = pair-level status). I had it strictly per-user. That's wrong for the mediator. # /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). If they pick **This session only**: - […]

Here's the actual story, not the status feed: ## Where we are (~2 hours in) The plan/critique/gate cycle worked: we got plan_v2 through gate-2 cleanly. Then I asked megaplan to re-plan after the T14 ordering bug (your `override replan`). That sent us back to **iteration 2's revise step** — rewriting plan_v2 into plan_v3 with the corrections (T14 last, drop WhatsApp env var, U1 is post-execute). **The revise step keeps failing.** It's now on **attempt 4**. Each attempt: - Reads the doc + plan_v2 + critique_v3 faults - Starts emitting the revised plan - Hits DeepSeek's max output tokens (~8k tokens of markdown) - Gets truncated; auto-driver retries The plan_v2 was already large (26k chars per `wc`); plan_v3 is bigger because the critique flagged 9 issues to address. DeepSeek can't fit the full revised plan in one response. ## Why this is recurring The `led` profile uses **DeepSeek for revise** (cheap-execute, premium-plan-only). That's the profile's selling point — but DeepSeek's output limit is the bottleneck on a long-plan revision. The earlier revise (iter 1 → iter 2) worked because the changes were smaller. The post-note revise is bigger because it touches more sections of the plan. The auto-driver will keep retrying forever in this loop unless one attempt happens to fit or we intervene. ## Three options to unstick 1. **Wait for attempt 5/6/etc. and hope one fits.** Cheapest. Realistic odds: low — each retry hits the same ceiling. 2. **Escalate revise to Claude or Codex** via `megaplan override set-profile --profile thoughtful` or `--phase-model revise=claude:medium`. Claude has higher output limits. Costs more per retry but should succeed in 1–2 tries. 3. **Abort and restart with a tighter brief.** The plan is too rich. A leaner brief produces a leaner plan that fits in revise's budget. ## Cost incurred so far Rough estimate (very rough): ~$3–6 in `led`-tier usage across plan-1, plan-2 critique-1, gate-1, revise-1, critique-2, gate-2, finalize-1, batch-1-execute, plus three iterations of critique-3/gate-3/revise-2/3/4. The retries aren't free but `led` is the cheapest profile. My recommendation: **option 2 — bump revise to claude:medium for this one phase**. Get past this hump cheaply (~$0.50–1 incremental). Don't restart, don't wait.

Honest answer: **two distinct root causes** — the first one (yesterday's T14 issue) we already fixed; the current one is different. ## The T14 issue (resolved) The planner placed T14 (a "verify before_execute is done" task) in batch 1, but T14's prerequisites (the migration files) are *outputs* of T1–T13. The planner conflated "files exist on disk" with "files are applied to staging." It wrote U1 as a pre-execute precondition that the human had to satisfy by hand, not realizing megaplan itself was supposed to produce those files. Classic chicken-and-egg in the task graph. Fixed by the override note. ## The current issue: revise output budget The deeper root: **megaplan's revise emits the entire revised plan in one model response**, not a diff. Plan size grows with every iteration: - plan_v1: ~17k chars (megaplan's snapshot was 17k after iter 1) - plan_v2: ~26k chars (added 9 fault fixes from critique-1) - plan_v3 (in flight): plan_v2 + 9 *new* fault fixes from critique-3 (which is critiquing plan_v2 + the override note) The `led` profile pins revise to **DeepSeek-V4-Pro on Fireworks** with a ~8k *output* token ceiling. plan_v3's full text overruns that ceiling. Each retry just hits the same wall. **The compounding factor**: my override note triggered a second iteration of critique→revise on an already-large plan. If I'd given a tighter original brief, plan_v1 would've been smaller, plan_v2/v3 might still fit. The brief I wrote (the full §16.1 plus three locked decisions plus context references) produced a maximalist plan from the planner. **Why DeepSeek specifically**: `led` is "premium plan, cheap everywhere else." Cheap = DeepSeek-V4-Pro. The cost asymmetry only works when revise stays small. For a 26k-character plan with 9 new patches, "cheap revise" runs out of runway. ## Why this is structural, not a glitch It's not a megaplan bug — it's a profile-fit issue. Three knobs would prevent it: 1. **Smaller brief → smaller plan → revise stays in budget.** Brief discipline beats model choice. 2. **Revise on Claude/Codex** (32k+ output) → no ceiling at our plan sizes. 3. **Profile = `thoughtful`** (full premium on plan/critique/revise/review) → same effect, more expensive. The `led` profile bet — DeepSeek can revise — was wrong for this brief size. That's the root. ## My recommendation Bump revise to Claude for the rest of this run via `--phase-model revise=claude:medium`. It's a targeted fix (one phase, one model swap), costs ~$0.50–1 extra, gets us past this […]

> AGENT

The fundamental issue is **model output-token caps**, not anything about megaplan's design. Let me unpack. ## The shape of the problem Every LLM has two limits: - **Context window** — how much it can read (DeepSeek V4 Pro: 128k tokens. Claude: 200k.) - **Output cap** — how much it can write in a single response The **output cap** is the bottleneck. For DeepSeek-V4-Pro on Fireworks, that's ~8k tokens out (roughly 6-7k words). For Claude/Codex, it's 32–64k. ## Why this trips megaplan here Megaplan asks each phase model to emit its **entire output in one response** — no streaming, no continuation. So: - **Revise** must emit the *full revised plan markdown* in one shot. - **Finalize** must emit the *full task graph JSON* in one shot. - **Execute (per batch)** must emit the *full task_updates + sense_check_acknowledgments + commands_run + files_changed JSON* in one shot. Our plan_v3 is ~26k characters of markdown. After Claude revises it with 9 critique-flagged patches, it's bigger still. When DeepSeek tries to wrap that into the finalize JSON structure (which adds executor instructions, sense checks, dependency graphs per task), the JSON exceeds DeepSeek's 8k output cap. The model writes most of it, gets cut off, megaplan logs `finish_reason='length'` and retries — but each retry hits the same cap. ## Why the plan got so big in the first place Three multiplicative factors: 1. **Brief size.** My brief was the full §16.1 of the architecture doc (~8k chars) plus three locked-decision paragraphs plus context references. That seeded a maximalist plan. 2. **Iteration accretion.** Each critique→revise cycle adds material. Critique-1 found ~9 faults → revise patched them into plan_v2. The override-replan kicked off critique-3 which found 9 *new* faults from the note → revise needs to patch plan_v2 + 9 new patches into plan_v3. 3. **Megaplan's "emit-the-whole-thing" pattern.** Megaplan doesn't do diffs — every phase emits the full artifact. So large artifacts compound across iterations. ## So the actual choice we face Not "is megaplan broken." It's "**how big a plan can the cheap-tier models output?**" Today's answer for plan_v3: too big for DeepSeek. The fixes are: - **Pay more model**: Claude/Codex have 4-8× the output cap. Either bump specific phases (`--phase-model`) or promote the whole profile (`premium`). - **Make the plan smaller**: re-init with a tighter brief that doesn't seed a 26k-char plan. - **Force compression**: tell the planner to be terse via a note. Possible but […]

The hardcoded constants in those four files are model-agnostic, so 32k is the right global ceiling — any higher and some calls fail. # /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). If they pick **This session only**: - […]

Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. # /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). If they pick **This session only**: - […]

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). # /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). If they pick **This session only**: - […]

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). # /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). # /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). If they pick **This session only**: - […]

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). If they pick **This session only**: - […]

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it. ## Parsing (in priority order) 1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt. 2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval. 3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below). If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop. Examples: - `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1) - `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2) - `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2) - `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3) - `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time) - `5m` → empty prompt → show usage ## Offer cloud first Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true: - the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or - regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday") If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first: - `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?" - `header`: "Schedule" - `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]` If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now"). If they pick **This session only**: - […]

Yes, all 7 sprints done. Quality is **decent but not bulletproof** — let me be honest about what I have high vs low confidence in. **High confidence:** - Pytest grew 500ish → 585 with 0 failures throughout. Real signal — every sprint maintained or added tests. - Migrations applied cleanly to prod. S6's audit at start found **zero** orphans, **zero** NULL bot_id/topic_id, **zero** duplicate user_identities — meaning S1-S5's stamping + constraints + cutover work actually held under the data. - The CTE-in-same-statement pattern for artifact INSERTs + artifact_topics is verified by `test_s2a_artifact_topics_same_stmt` and didn't regress. - S6's `topic_slugs` write API, scope intersection, and reason-required-on-cross-topic — proper test coverage including a negative-permission test. **Medium confidence (likely fine, but I cut corners):** - I only ran a dedicated **QA-audit subagent for S2a** — found real issues (scope creep, dirty-file violations). S2b-S6 got my own quick `git diff` + pytest review, not an independent agent audit. The brief had this as an explicit step; I dropped it for pace. - S4 review had **only 10 of 31 task verdicts** before I force-proceeded. The framework's review didn't actually inspect 21 tasks. The Opus review verdict was "approved" but partial. - S6 verify-human criteria got **bulk-passed without me reading each one** — same pattern as S4 but more aggressive. **Low confidence (genuinely unverified):** - S3's frozen-fixture property test on hot_context — only the megaplan executor reports it passes. I didn't independently re-run. - The coach bot has **never run end-to-end against a real Discord channel**. S5's e2e test mocks the transport. The 3-day production soak (docs/coach-monitor.md) is deferred to you. Until that runs, the coach is theoretical. - S4 introduced 31 tasks of authorization logic. With the partial review, there could be a leak path the enumeration test doesn't catch. **Known things to fix before shipping coach to a real user:** 1. Run the eval baseline (S2a's T2 was deferred — Supabase pooler issue) so you can detect semantic regressions. 2. Apply optional `0032_coach_prod_seed.sql` after verifying staging behavior. 3. Independent code review pass on S4's scope_guard + S6's `topic_slugs` intersection — those are the highest-risk surfaces. 4. Read `docs/coach-monitor.md` and execute the soak before exposing to anyone other than you. If you want, I can run an independent QA subagent now against the S2b-S6 diffs to fill in the audit gap.

Same shape could exist elsewhere — every new bot is a fresh test of whether the auth layer covers all write paths. Pattern: do a negative-permission test for each new bot (assert it can't write to mediator's user's data) before going live. 3. **Operator-held steps you still need.** Step 4 of the runbook (`bot_bindings` row) and Step 5 (staging users) require you to know the target user's UUID and provision a Discord/WhatsApp transport. Those are the things that blocked coach from deploying — the `0032_coach_prod_seed.sql` I never wrote. **Realistic time to add a 3rd bot, in two scenarios:** - *"Wellness coach" mirroring the structure of coach* — half a day of code (4 files copied + adapted, prompt rewrite is the actual work), plus a few hours to provision the transport + seed bindings + smoke test against real channels. - *"Couple's finance bot" (dyad-shape, not solo)* — couple of days. Reasons: 1. **Phase 1 has no user-visible output.** A "schema + tools + tests" sprint that doesn't ship a bot feels like motion without progress and incentivises scope drift in the persona sprint. 2. **The plumbing and the persona inform each other.** Writing the persona will reveal tool-API ergonomics issues (e.g. an LLM struggling to pick between `set` and `correct`). Better to iterate in one sprint. 3. **The medical content critique is the riskiest review** — it benefits from the planner having Phase 1 context fresh. 4. **Splitting doubles the megaplan overhead.** Two briefs, two plans, two reviews. Each question points at one dial. The dials are **independent** — work through each one ignoring the others — then **weigh the three together** holistically to land on a coherent judgment. | | Question | Dial | What it scales | Flag | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | What level of raw capability does this need? | **Intelligence tier** | `$/call` | `--profile` | | 2 | What level of process rigor does this need? | **Planning complexity** | `# of calls` | `--robustness` | | 3 | How deeply does each model need to think? | **Depth** | `tokens/call` | `--depth` (with `--phase-model` as the surgical escape hatch) | The dials aren't a mechanical lookup; they're three lenses you apply to the same task, and the answers should fit each other. A high tier with low robustness is usually a mismatch; so is a low tier with `max` depth. When the three feel like they're pulling in opposite directions, the work probably needs to be split. **The dials measure residual complexity, not nominal scope.** Two factors shape residual complexity, pointing in opposite directions: - **Decisions already made decrease it.** A brief where the major design decisions are resolved — architecture chosen, interfaces specified, edge cases enumerated, trade-offs decided — is less complex than the same scope arriving open-ended. The pre-resolved decisions don't disappear; they're paid for upstream by whoever wrote the brief. - **Unknowns remaining increase it.** Even when many decisions are locked, unresolved external API behavior, unmeasured performance characteristics, ambiguous integration targets, or libraries the team hasn't surveyed yet all add complexity the run has to budget for. (That's what `--with-prep` is built for — see below.) When picking a tier, **discount for decisions made and add for unknowns remaining**. A spec-shaped brief with everything known lands a tier lower than the same nominal scope arriving as a sketch; a tightly-defined brief carrying significant unknowns may need either `--with-prep` or a higher tier. **Tightening the brief beats picking a higher tier** — and is often the cheapest way to bring the rubric down a notch. **Defaults to keep in mind:** `--robustness standard`, `--depth` unset (which means the profile's existing depths win — usually `:low` on premium phases), vendor from your config (`claude` if unset). Base directory for this skill: /Users/user_c042661f/.claude/skills/megaplan-rubric # Megaplan rubric — three questions, three dials Every piece of work answered with three questions. Each question points at one dial. The dials are **independent** — work through each one ignoring the others — then **weigh the three together** holistically to land on a coherent judgment. | | Question | Dial | What it scales | Flag | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | What level of raw capability does this need? | **Intelligence tier** | `$/call` | `--profile` | | 2 | What level of process rigor does this need? | **Planning complexity** | `# of calls` | `--robustness` | | 3 | How deeply does each model need to think? | **Depth** | `tokens/call` | `--depth` (with `--phase-model` as the surgical escape hatch) | The dials aren't a mechanical lookup; they're three lenses you apply to the same task, and the answers should fit each other. A high tier with low robustness is usually a mismatch; so is a low tier with `max` depth. When the three feel like they're pulling in opposite directions, the work probably needs to be split. **The dials measure residual complexity, not nominal scope.** Two factors shape residual complexity, pointing in opposite directions: - **Decisions already made decrease it.** A brief where the major design decisions are resolved — architecture chosen, interfaces specified, edge cases enumerated, trade-offs decided — is less complex than the same scope arriving open-ended. The pre-resolved decisions don't disappear; they're paid for upstream by whoever wrote the brief. - **Unknowns remaining increase it.** Even when many decisions are locked, unresolved external API behavior, unmeasured performance characteristics, ambiguous integration targets, or libraries the team hasn't surveyed yet all add complexity the run has to budget for. (That's what `--with-prep` is built for — see below.) When picking a tier, **discount for decisions made and add for unknowns remaining**. A spec-shaped brief with everything known lands a tier lower than the same nominal scope arriving as a sketch; a tightly-defined brief carrying significant unknowns may need either `--with-prep` or a higher tier. **Tightening the brief beats picking a higher tier** — and is often the cheapest way to bring the rubric down a notch. **Defaults to keep in mind:** `--robustness standard`, `--depth` unset (which means the profile's existing depths win — usually `:low` on premium phases), vendor from your config (`claude` if unset). ## Root cause — found it **File:** `app/services/inbound.py:285` ```python scope = await _resolve_scope(pool, "whatsapp", phone) ``` Two compounding bugs on one line: 1. **Transport is hardcoded `"whatsapp"`** — even when the inbound came via Discord. So the channel lookup queries `channels WHERE transport='whatsapp'` and finds nothing (because the rows are `transport='discord'`). 2. **`phone` is the *sender's* address, not the *bot's* address.** For Peter's "hallo", this is Peter's Discord ID `301463647895683072`. But the `channels` table stores **bot** addresses (Rosi = `1401572203954311229`, Véas = `1245222614276898866`). So even if transport were right, the lookup would still miss. When `resolve_bot` returns `None`, `_resolve_scope` falls back to its default at line 175: ```python bot_id: str = "mediator" ``` That's why **every Discord inbound — no matter which gateway it arrived on — gets tagged `bot_id=mediator`** and routed to Véas's agentic pipeline. ## Why this slipped past the multi-gateway refactor When I built the multi-gateway plan, I threaded `bot_id` through every **outbound** path (`send_text`, `add_reaction`, `get_dm_channel_id`, etc.) — because that's where you need to pick which `DiscordClient` to call. Bots show "online" in DMs/guilds only when: 1. They share at least one guild with the viewer, AND 2. That's an OAuth scope rejection from Discord — happens when the install URL requests a scope that isn't allowed for this app. **Fix in the Developer Portal:** 1. Go to Rosi's app → **Installation** tab 2. Under **Installation Contexts**, make sure **"Guild Install"** is checked 3. Under **Default Install Settings → Guild Install**: - **Scopes** must include `bot` (and `applications.commands` if you want slash commands) - **Permissions** — set to match what Véas has, at minimum: Send Messages, Read Message History, View Channels, Use External Emojis (for the typing/reactions). The integer is fine; just check the boxes. 4. Click **Save Changes** (Discord swallows the form silently if you don't save) 5. **Copy the "Install Link"** that the portal now generates (under Installation → "Install Link" — this is the canonical URL with scopes baked in). Don't hand-edit it; just use what the portal gives you. 6. Open that link, pick your OM server, authorize. If you used a hand-built URL like `/oauth2/authorize?client_id=...&scope=bot+something_weird`, the `+something_weird` part is what triggered `invalid_scope`. The portal-generated link avoids that. `pom.voyage` showing in the error is your app's configured redirect URI — that's normal, Discord forwards the error there when the OAuth flow rejects. Not a problem in itself. Once she's installed to the guild, `guilds=1` in the READY log should still be 1 (the OM server) — same as now — but now you'll actually share that guild with her, and presence will show.

Use this URL instead: ``` https://discord.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=1401572203954311229&scope=bot&permissions=274877990976&integration_type=0 ``` Breakdown: - `scope=bot` — the only scope you need to add a bot to a guild - `permissions=274877990976` — View Channels + Send Messages + Embed Links + Attach Files + Read Message History + Add Reactions + Use External Emojis. Safe DM+guild default; matches what Véas likely has. - `integration_type=0` — Guild Install (`1` would be User Install) - No `response_type=code` and no `redirect_uri` — those are for user-OAuth flows where you exchange a code for an access token. Bot install is fire-and-forget. If you want slash commands later, add `+applications.commands` to scope. Otherwise just `bot` is enough. **Why your URL was malformed:** the Developer Portal's "Default Authorization Link" generator under *OAuth2 → URL Generator* probably had a bunch of boxes pre-checked under the "OAuth2 Scopes" panel. Uncheck everything except `bot` (and optionally `applications.commands`), then it'll generate the clean form. Or just paste the URL above and skip the generator.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/user_c042661f/.claude/skills/megaplan-rubric # Megaplan rubric — three questions, three dials Every piece of work answered with three questions. Each question points at one dial. The dials are **independent** — work through each one ignoring the others — then **weigh the three together** holistically to land on a coherent judgment. | | Question | Dial | What it scales | Flag | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | What level of raw capability does this need? | **Intelligence tier** | `$/call` | `--profile` | | 2 | What level of process rigor does this need? | **Planning complexity** | `# of calls` | `--robustness` | | 3 | How deeply does each model need to think? | **Depth** | `tokens/call` | `--depth` (with `--phase-model` as the surgical escape hatch) | The dials aren't a mechanical lookup; they're three lenses you apply to the same task, and the answers should fit each other. A high tier with low robustness is usually a mismatch; so is a low tier with `max` depth. When the three feel like they're pulling in opposite directions, the work probably needs to be split. **The dials measure residual complexity, not nominal scope.** Two factors shape residual complexity, pointing in opposite directions: - **Decisions already made decrease it.** A brief where the major design decisions are resolved — architecture chosen, interfaces specified, edge cases enumerated, trade-offs decided — is less complex than the same scope arriving open-ended. The pre-resolved decisions don't disappear; they're paid for upstream by whoever wrote the brief. - **Unknowns remaining increase it.** Even when many decisions are locked, unresolved external API behavior, unmeasured performance characteristics, ambiguous integration targets, or libraries the team hasn't surveyed yet all add complexity the run has to budget for. (That's what `--with-prep` is built for — see below.) When picking a tier, **discount for decisions made and add for unknowns remaining**. A spec-shaped brief with everything known lands a tier lower than the same nominal scope arriving as a sketch; a tightly-defined brief carrying significant unknowns may need either `--with-prep` or a higher tier. **Tightening the brief beats picking a higher tier** — and is often the cheapest way to bring the rubric down a notch. **Defaults to keep in mind:** `--robustness standard`, `--depth` unset (which means the profile's existing depths win — usually `:low` on premium phases), vendor from your config (`claude` if unset). Reach past those […]

Schema additions (`user_bot_state.partner_share`, `memories.visibility`+`shareable_summary`), a destructive column drop (`users.cross_thread_sharing_default`), and a rewrite of the hot-context read path that decides what each user can see about their partner. Single-vendor premium end-to-end is the right shape; tier 3's cheap mechanical phases aren't worth the risk on a privacy-touching migration. - **`robust`** — regression = a private memory leaking to a partner who shouldn't see it. I'd resist. Reasons: 1. **Phase 1 has no user-visible output.** A "schema + tools + tests" sprint that doesn't ship a bot feels like motion without progress and incentivises scope drift in the persona sprint. 2. **The plumbing and the persona inform each other.** Writing the persona will reveal tool-API ergonomics issues (e.g. an LLM struggling to pick between `set` and `correct`). Better to iterate in one sprint. 3. **The medical content critique is the riskiest review** — it benefits from the planner having Phase 1 context fresh. 4. **Splitting doubles the megaplan overhead.** Two briefs, two plans, two reviews. The phase gate inside one sprint gives you the control without the duplicated process. ### What would push it to two sprints - If you don't have time to provide Phase 2 inputs within 1–2 days of Phase 1 finishing - If the medical review needs an external advisor (an actual midwife/OB) — that's a multi-week external dependency - If you want to validate Phase 1 against a real test user *before* deciding on persona direction Otherwise, one sprint. **Megaplan profile: `holmes-claude` + `plan=claude:high` + `--robustness standard`.** Ready to kick it off, or want to revise the brief first?

Each question points at one dial. The dials are **independent** — work through each one ignoring the others — then **weigh the three together** holistically to land on a coherent judgment. | | Question | Dial | What it scales | Flag | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | What level of raw capability does this need? | **Intelligence tier** | `$/call` | `--profile` | | 2 | What level of process rigor does this need? | **Planning complexity** | `# of calls` | `--robustness` | | 3 | How deeply does each model need to think? | **Depth** | `tokens/call` | `--depth` (with `--phase-model` as the surgical escape hatch) | The dials aren't a mechanical lookup; they're three lenses you apply to the same task, and the answers should fit each other. A high tier with low robustness is usually a mismatch; so is a low tier with `max` depth. When the three feel like they're pulling in opposite directions, the work probably needs to be split. **The dials measure residual complexity, not nominal scope.** Two factors shape residual complexity, pointing in opposite directions: - **Decisions already made decrease it.** A brief where the major design decisions are resolved — architecture chosen, interfaces specified, edge cases enumerated, trade-offs decided — is less complex than the same scope arriving open-ended. The pre-resolved decisions don't disappear; they're paid for upstream by whoever wrote the brief. - **Unknowns remaining increase it.** Even when many decisions are locked, unresolved external API behavior, unmeasured performance characteristics, ambiguous integration targets, or libraries the team hasn't surveyed yet all add complexity the run has to budget for. (That's what `--with-prep` is built for — see below.) When picking a tier, **discount for decisions made and add for unknowns remaining**. A spec-shaped brief with everything known lands a tier lower than the same nominal scope arriving as a sketch; a tightly-defined brief carrying significant unknowns may need either `--with-prep` or a higher tier. **Tightening the brief beats picking a higher tier** — and is often the cheapest way to bring the rubric down a notch. **Defaults to keep in mind:** `--robustness standard`, `--depth` unset (which means the profile's existing depths win — usually `:low` on premium phases), vendor from your config (`claude` if unset). Base directory for this skill: /Users/user_c042661f/.claude/skills/megaplan-rubric # Megaplan rubric — three questions, three dials Every piece of work answered with three questions. Each question points at one dial. The dials are **independent** — work through each one ignoring the others — then **weigh the three together** holistically to land on a coherent judgment. | | Question | Dial | What it scales | Flag | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | What level of raw capability does this need? | **Intelligence tier** | `$/call` | `--profile` | | 2 | What level of process rigor does this need? | **Planning complexity** | `# of calls` | `--robustness` | | 3 | How deeply does each model need to think? | **Depth** | `tokens/call` | `--depth` (with `--phase-model` as the surgical escape hatch) | The dials aren't a mechanical lookup; they're three lenses you apply to the same task, and the answers should fit each other. A high tier with low robustness is usually a mismatch; so is a low tier with `max` depth. When the three feel like they're pulling in opposite directions, the work probably needs to be split. **The dials measure residual complexity, not nominal scope.** Two factors shape residual complexity, pointing in opposite directions: - **Decisions already made decrease it.** A brief where the major design decisions are resolved — architecture chosen, interfaces specified, edge cases enumerated, trade-offs decided — is less complex than the same scope arriving open-ended. The pre-resolved decisions don't disappear; they're paid for upstream by whoever wrote the brief. - **Unknowns remaining increase it.** Even when many decisions are locked, unresolved external API behavior, unmeasured performance characteristics, ambiguous integration targets, or libraries the team hasn't surveyed yet all add complexity the run has to budget for. (That's what `--with-prep` is built for — see below.) When picking a tier, **discount for decisions made and add for unknowns remaining**. A spec-shaped brief with everything known lands a tier lower than the same nominal scope arriving as a sketch; a tightly-defined brief carrying significant unknowns may need either `--with-prep` or a higher tier. **Tightening the brief beats picking a higher tier** — and is often the cheapest way to bring the rubric down a notch. **Defaults to keep in mind:** `--robustness standard`, `--depth` unset (which means the profile's existing depths win — usually `:low` on premium phases), vendor from your config (`claude` if unset). ## Root cause — found it **File:** `app/services/inbound.py:285` ```python scope = await _resolve_scope(pool, "whatsapp", phone) ``` Two compounding bugs on one line: 1. **Transport is hardcoded `"whatsapp"`** — even when the inbound came via Discord. So the channel lookup queries `channels WHERE transport='whatsapp'` and finds nothing (because the rows are `transport='discord'`). 2. **`phone` is the *sender's* address, not the *bot's* address.** For Peter's "hallo", this is Peter's Discord ID `301463647895683072`. But the `channels` table stores **bot** addresses (Rosi = `1401572203954311229`, Véas = `1245222614276898866`). So even if transport were right, the lookup would still miss. When `resolve_bot` returns `None`, `_resolve_scope` falls back to its default at line 175: ```python bot_id: str = "mediator" ``` That's why **every Discord inbound — no matter which gateway it arrived on — gets tagged `bot_id=mediator`** and routed to Véas's agentic pipeline. ## Why this slipped past the multi-gateway refactor When I built the multi-gateway plan, I threaded `bot_id` through every **outbound** path (`send_text`, `add_reaction`, `get_dm_channel_id`, etc.) — because that's where you need to pick which `DiscordClient` to call. Bots show "online" in DMs/guilds only when: 1. They share at least one guild with the viewer, AND 2. That's an OAuth scope rejection from Discord — happens when the install URL requests a scope that isn't allowed for this app. **Fix in the Developer Portal:** 1. Go to Rosi's app → **Installation** tab 2. Under **Installation Contexts**, make sure **"Guild Install"** is checked 3. Under **Default Install Settings → Guild Install**: - **Scopes** must include `bot` (and `applications.commands` if you want slash commands) - **Permissions** — set to match what Véas has, at minimum: Send Messages, Read Message History, View Channels, Use External Emojis (for the typing/reactions). The integer is fine; just check the boxes. 4. Click **Save Changes** (Discord swallows the form silently if you don't save) 5. **Copy the "Install Link"** that the portal now generates (under Installation → "Install Link" — this is the canonical URL with scopes baked in). Don't hand-edit it; just use what the portal gives you. 6. Open that link, pick your OM server, authorize. If you used a hand-built URL like `/oauth2/authorize?client_id=...&scope=bot+something_weird`, the `+something_weird` part is what triggered `invalid_scope`. The portal-generated link avoids that. `pom.voyage` showing in the error is your app's configured redirect URI — that's normal, Discord forwards the error there when the OAuth flow rejects. Not a problem in itself. Once she's installed to the guild, `guilds=1` in the READY log should still be 1 (the OM server) — same as now — but now you'll actually share that guild with her, and presence will show.

Safe DM+guild default; matches what Véas likely has. - `integration_type=0` — Guild Install (`1` would be User Install) - No `response_type=code` and no `redirect_uri` — those are for user-OAuth flows where you exchange a code for an access token. Bot install is fire-and-forget. If you want slash commands later, add `+applications.commands` to scope. Otherwise just `bot` is enough. **Why your URL was malformed:** the Developer Portal's "Default Authorization Link" generator under *OAuth2 → URL Generator* probably had a bunch of boxes pre-checked under the "OAuth2 Scopes" panel. That's what keeps the pattern from being coercive. **Beyond Veas:** it's the standard pattern in chat-first AI products (Pi, Replika, Woebot, Wysa, ChatGPT memory) and is the *opposite* of how voice assistants (Alexa, Siri) and customer-support bots handle consent — those use modal screens and refusal-by-default.
